job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Jamal Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Jamal, thanks for coming. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group that has no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Ha, it's a bit of a patchwork. I'm doing a master's in mechatronics at Northgate, which is mechanical engineering mixed with electronics and control. I share a flat with two lads, we argue about whose turn it is to buy bin bags. Weekends I work at a bike shop on Canal Street, fixing gears and brakes, which I honestly love.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mechanical engineering, a pass. My final project was a test rig for gearboxes, and it mostly worked, which my supervisor called a win. No internship, because the summer I should've done one my gran was ill and I stayed home to help. I don't regret it, though it doesn't show on a CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's about what I thought. I use a chatbot now and again to tidy my reports, and it's handy, but it isn't running anything. At the bike shop it changes nothing at all, a puncture is a puncture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means the job hunt is the same as before. Mechanical firms near Northgate do take graduates, but they take the ones with internships first. I'd keep wondering if I'm the last in the queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and put my gearbox rig and a mechatronics project on my CV. I'd apply to about six firms a month, including the pump maker and the lift company. I'd keep the bike shop, and I'd ask the owner, Reggie, to write me a reference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, a bit meh. Like waiting for a bus that's late but will turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the bike shop reference say that a degree can't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I turn up, I'm honest with customers and I fix things properly. Reggie once let me handle a whole wheel rebuild alone. A reference from a man who trusts me with a customer's bike counts for more than a mark on a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are the pressures you carry here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About 12,000 of loan, and the fact that my mum's nail salon has been quieter this year. She'd never ask me for money but I can see the books. I'd like to be earning before she has to say anything.

At the bike shop it changes **nothing**: a puncture is a puncture.
think: The job hunt is the same as before and internships go **first**.
My mum's **salon** has been quieter, which adds pressure.
do: **Put** the gearbox rig and a mechatronics project on my CV.
**Apply** to about six firms a month, including a pump maker.
Ask **Reggie** (the bike shop owner) for a reference.
feel: **Meh**, like waiting for a late bus that will turn up.
S0.quote: A reference from a man who trusts me with a customer's bike counts for more than a mark on a certificate.
fieldNote: Easygoing voice, but the pressure comes from his **mother's** quiet salon.

Values **trust** from a bike shop owner over grades.

steps.text: Add the gearbox rig and a mechatronics project to the CV
Apply to six engineering firms a month near Northgate
Keep the Saturday and Sunday bike shop shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change some desk jobs but I'd wait to see the proof. If the tools really do take over the calculations and drawings, firms will hire fewer people to do those. I'd tell my flatmates to get comfortable with them, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it makes the entry jobs smaller. Mechanical roles are half desk and half workshop, and the desk half is what gets squeezed. I'm not terrified, but I notice the job ads asking for more skills for the same junior pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the tools properly for my project reports and CAD checks, so I know them before an employer asks. I'd aim for roles with a workshop element, like testing or commissioning. And I'd use the bike shop more as a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit tense. It's a slow squeeze, not a punch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's a role with a workshop element?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Commissioning, where you set up a machine at a customer's site and make it run. Or test engineering. They need hands as well as brains. I'd rather stand next to a running machine than sit in front of a screen that a program can replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who worries you at work in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My flatmate Dev, who does software. He thinks he's safe because he's good, but juniors like him are who the card describes. I told him to start networking now. He laughed, but he did it.

I'd tell flatmates to get **comfortable** with them.

fieldNote: Steady: he acts once the change looks **proven**, and starts early enough.
Hedges with **hands-on** roles and a workshop job.
Worries for a software flatmate who feels **safe**.

steps.text: Use an AI assistant to check CAD reports and calculations
Apply for commissioning and test engineer jobs
Take extra shifts at the bike shop when applications are slow

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is mad. Nobody can plan for that, not firms, not schools, not families. I'd tell people to speak to their local councillor and not leave it to the big names.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be scared. By the time I finish the master's, the thinking jobs would be going. Hands-on work gives me three more years than a desk worker, but I've no idea what happens after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd skip the engineering hunt and look for work that's physical, like workshop technician or bike mechanic full time. I'd save every pound I can, and I'd stay at the flat with the lads because sharing costs less. I'd also ask Mum what the salon's books look like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Like carrying a wet coat all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really give up engineering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not give up, park it. The degree doesn't vanish, it just stops being the front door. I'd rather fix gears for a living than wait two years for an engineering job that might not exist. I'd keep a foot in with side projects.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we should look at what we've got together and plan for the worst. She'd tell me not to worry, and I'd say we both should, a bit. We'd probably end up laughing about it, but we'd do the sums.

say: Two years is **mad**; nobody can plan for it.
Speak to your local **councillor** and don't leave it to big names.
think: The thinking jobs would go before I **start**.
Hands-on work gives **three more years**, but nothing is clear after.
do: **Look** for full-time workshop technician or bike mechanic work.
**Save** every pound and stay in the shared flat.
Ask Mum how the salon's **books** look.
feel: **Heavy**, like carrying a wet coat all day.
S2.quote: I'd rather fix gears for a living than wait two years for an engineering job that might not exist.
fieldNote: Steady and practical: **parks** engineering and chooses hands-on work.
Wants to **plan** with his mother, a family-first reflex.
Humour stays, but the weight is **real**.

steps.text: Apply for full-time workshop technician and bike mechanic jobs
Save every spare pound in a separate account
Stay in the shared flat and cut takeaway spending
Sit down with Mum and go through the salon's books

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to build something but short enough to take seriously. I'd tell mates to learn a trade skill alongside the degree, as a belt and braces thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd get a first job, work two or three years, and have a bit of a cushion. A mechatronics graduate who can fix real machines should be fine for the robot years. Three years after AGI is a long time to be useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply hard for commissioning roles and take the first decent one. I'd save about 250 a month and start paying the loan down faster. I'd also do a short course in industrial robots, since someone will have to install and mend them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reasonably okay. I'd say a seven out of ten on the worry scale, if ten is panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why robots as the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if they're coming around 2034, someone has to put them in and fix them, and I'm already a mechanical and electronics person. Every robot that replaces a worker still needs a human with a spanner at the end of the day. I'd be that human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the thinking side of mechatronics?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The programming part will go to the tools first, I'd guess. I'd let them do it and I'd check the output on the real machine. It's a good way to work, honestly.

say: Five years is long enough to **build** something but still serious.
Learn a **trade skill** alongside the degree as belt and braces.
think: A mechatronics graduate who fixes real machines should do **fine**.
Three years after AGI is **long** enough to stay useful.
do: **Apply** for commissioning roles and take the first decent one.
**Save** 250 a month and pay the loan down faster.
Take a **short course** in industrial robots.
feel: **Reasonably okay**, about seven out of ten on the worry scale.
S3.quote: Every robot that replaces a worker still needs a human with a spanner at the end of the day.
fieldNote: Sees himself on the **right side** of the robot gap with a trade angle.
Jokes about a worry scale but still names a **seven**.

steps.text: Take the first commissioning engineer job on offer
Save 250 a month and put extra toward the loan
Take a short course in installing industrial robots
Use AI for programming drafts and test them on the machine

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd be silly not to use it. I'd tell people to pick up one skill that's useful whoever's in charge, like fixing things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fairly calm. By 34 I could have ten years in engineering, maybe a flat, and be someone who knows machines. If robots come in 2039 I'd already be working with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any engineering job and work my way up. I'd buy a place with a mate or a partner when the loan is cleared. And I'd keep the bike shop as a hobby, so I have something that isn't a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easy, mostly. A good long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hobby bike shop for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's my reality check. If everything online went strange, I'd still know how to fix a chain. I like having a skill that doesn't need a login, and a bike with a bent wheel doesn't care what year it is. It's a bit of insurance with grease on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any worry left?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum's salon, to be honest, and my gran's health. Not AI, just life. Those are the things I'd lose sleep over, and no scenario changes them.

think: By 34 I could have **ten years** in engineering and a flat.
If robots come in 2039 I'd already be **working with them**.
do: **Take** any engineering job and work upward.
**Buy** a place once the loan is cleared.
Keep the **bike shop** as a screen-free hobby.
feel: **Easy**, mostly, with a good long runway.
S4.quote: I like having a skill that doesn't need a login, and a bike with a bent wheel doesn't care what year it is.
fieldNote: Long runway matches his **steady** style and he relaxes visibly.

steps.text: Take the first engineering job and work upward

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because I'd have a gap between finishing and anything useful. What would help is some kind of guaranteed first job or paid training for new graduates, and honest advice about which skills hold up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much of this is about families, not careers. My mum's salon, my gran's health and my loan all happen on the same weekend, and no scenario knows that.

headlineQuote: My mum's salon, my gran's health and my loan all happen on the same weekend, and no scenario knows that.
portrait: Jamal is 24, doing a **mechatronics** master's after a pass in mechanical engineering.
He shares a flat in **Northgate** and works weekends at a bike shop.
Centrist and steady, he uses AI **now and then** and acts once changes look proven.
His shelter is **hands-on** work, and a part-time workshop job keeps him grounded.
He carries about 12,000 in loan and worries about his mother's **quiet salon**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because of the gap before any useful work.
whatWouldHelp: A **guaranteed first job** or paid training, plus honest advice on skills.
